Those are incommensurable quantities, and the right axis differs across panels (0–25 for Black, Hispanic, Asian, SWD and ELL; 40–65 for Female; 55–80 for White). The sentence 'while Hispanic/Latino students exhibit higher representation among Chapter 74 participants relative to their population share, the narrowing of this gap over time indicates that their participation has not scaled in proportion to their demographic increase' sits immediately beside panel (e), where the gray population line visibly rises through and past the black participation line around 2018. A reader will naturally take that crossing as the evidence. It is not — the crossing of a rate against a share has no representation interpretation. The claim is in fact defensible, but only by comparing panel (e)'s black line to panel (a)'s black line (roughly 18→19.8 against 15→19.2, a representation ratio of about 1.2 falling to about 1.03), or by consulting Figure A4, which is where the text actually points and which readers of the article cannot see.

The characterization of the raw ELL trend as 'relatively flat' is also loose. Panel (h) shows ELL participation dipping from about 12.8 in 2010 to about 12.9 around 2018 and then rising sharply to about 15.9 by 2024, with concentration moving from about 9.6 to about 12.1. Read against panel (a), ELLs sit modestly and fairly stably below parity across the whole period — which, interestingly, is the raw pattern the abstract's word 'persistent' would fit, even though the abstract attaches that word to the within-school mechanism, where the body says the opposite. The final two cohorts also show the ELL population share falling from about 9 to about 7 percent while ELL participation rises, a compositional break that goes unremarked.

Two panels get no prose at all. Students with disabilities (panel g) are the most over-represented group in the data — participation around 23 percent against a population share around 16 — with an essentially flat adjusted coefficient (slope -0.0002, not significant). Asian students (panel f) are the most under-represented, at about 10.7 percent participation against an overall rate of about 19. Neither appears anywhere in the text. That is defensible triage in a brief, but a reader should know that two of the eight panels are unaccompanied by any interpretation.

FIDELITY, FIGURE 2. This figure is the paper's argument, and it is drawn honestly: point estimates, 95 percent intervals, a fitted line, and a printed slope with stars in each of six panels. Panel (a) Female runs from about -0.0135 in 2010 to about -0.0065 in 2023, slope 0.0006 (p<.01), with every interval — including the last two — excluding zero. Panel (b) Black runs from about -0.0155 to about -0.012 with wide intervals throughout, slope 0.0005 (p<.05). Panel (c) Hispanic/Latino runs from about -0.013 to about -0.001, crossing zero around 2018 and touching +0.0055 in 2021, slope 0.0011 (p<.01), but with visible reversals (about -0.014 in 2013, about -0.017 in 2014). Panel (d) Asian and panel (e) SWD are flat (0.0002 and -0.0002, neither starred). Panel (f) ELL runs from about -0.004 in 2010 — with an interval spanning roughly +0.008 to -0.016, comfortably including zero, and a 2013 point that is positive at about +0.0037 — down to about -0.022 in 2023, slope -0.0010 (p<.05, the weakest significance among the three starred panels).

That reading matters for two sentences. First, 'For female and Hispanic/Latino students, the negative association with Chapter 74 concentration within schools and towns has steadily converged toward zero' is true of Hispanic students and not of female students, whose gap shrinks by roughly 0.7 percentage points but never becomes statistically indistinguishable from zero. Lumping the two obscures a real difference, and the Discussion's more careful 'their more muted adjusted coefficients' is the phrasing to trust. 'Steadily' overstates both series. Second, the ELL story: because the 2010 baseline is imprecise and centered near zero, 'widened' is a claim about a trend line fitted through very noisy early estimates, and the abstract's 'persistent' is not merely a synonym for it but its opposite in temporal structure.

Self-containment fails in one important respect. Figure 2 drops the Overall and White panels that Figure 1 has. The race coefficients are therefore relative to an unnamed omitted category, and the note says only that models control for 'all major student demographics.' There is no way for a reader to establish the comparison group from the article. The note also says the models control for 'baseline math achievement,' where the text says 'baseline academic achievement,' and says 'Grade 9 school fixed effect' where the text says 'high school' fixed effects. Neither discrepancy is fatal, but a reader who quotes the text will overstate the controls.

THE COHORT MISMATCH. Figure 1's note and axes cover 2010–2024; Figure 2's cover 2010–2023. The title, abstract and Data section all say fifteen cohorts and 2010 through 2024. Nothing acknowledges the dropped year. The most likely explanation is that Grade 8 baseline measures, which Figure 2 conditions on, are unavailable for the 2024 graduating cohort because those students were in Grade 8 in spring 2020 — but the pandemic is not mentioned anywhere in the paper. The omission is consequential rather than cosmetic: 2024 is the cohort in which Figure 1(e) shows Hispanic/Latino participation dropping from about 21 to about 19.8 and concentration from about 17.9 to about 15.8, the single largest movement in the figure. The adjusted analysis excludes its own most volatile year, silently.

RHETORICAL DRIFT. The design is a linear probability model with Grade 9 school and town-of-residence fixed effects plus controls, run separately by cohort. The paper describes it as letting them 'isolate the net association,' calls it a 'decomposition approach' (nothing is decomposed), identifies 'the potential driver' of the Hispanic pattern, declares that for Hispanic students 'access to the programs remains the critical lever,' and uses 'barriers' in the abstract and twice in the Discussion. The abstract's 'appears tied to their school access and choice' and 'face persistent within-school barriers' will be read by a policy audience as mechanism claims. The inference rule the paper states — 'If raw disparities were driven largely by program supply and access, these estimates would remain small across cohorts' — is offered once and its output is then treated as settled; non-small estimates are equally consistent with within-school unobservables, with time-varying ELL classification (an endogenous, reclassifiable status that is never discussed), or with the achievement control absorbing the rationing channel. On that last point the paper supplies the tension itself: it reports (Figure A2) that baseline achievement among entrants rose as demand rose, and then conditions Figure 2 on Grade 8 math. If selection operates on prior achievement, the adjusted coefficient is a residual gap among observationally similar students rather than a gap in access — precisely the reading the word 'barriers' discourages.

DEPENDENCE ON INVISIBLE EXHIBITS. Nine of the eleven exhibits referenced are online-only, and they are not decoration. A7 (the within-Hispanic ELL result, with the parenthetical that Hispanic students are about two-thirds of ELLs) is what licenses the paper's central move from ethnicity to language. A8 (expansion concentrated in education and health services, which demand more English) is the entire proposed mechanism for the ELL finding. A9 (Perkins-only concentrators show muted associations and no cohort trend) is what licenses the closing claim that inequity is 'a more distinctive feature of high-quality pathways.' Each is one sentence with no numbers. A6 (Grade 8 school fixed effects) is the robustness check that supports the residential-sorting interpretation for Hispanic students. A reader of the article alone cannot evaluate any of the paper's three headline interpretations.

TERMINOLOGY. 'High-quality' does the heaviest lifting of any phrase in the paper — it is in the title, the abstract, every Results and Discussion paragraph, and the closing claim. It is established only by inputs (900 hours, employer partnerships, credential opportunity) and the assertion that 'this distinction signals a "quality premium"' — scare-quoted once, never returned to, never supported by outcome evidence in the body. Readers should substitute 'Chapter 74–approved' throughout and judge the closing claim accordingly.

MINOR PRODUCTION LAPSES. The Acknowledgments begin 'We also gratefully acknowledge,' which implies a preceding sentence was cut. 'Chapter74' is unspaced in the Figure 1 title. Panel labels read 'English language Learners' in Figure 1 and 'English Language Learners' in Figure 2. Cross-references use a nonstandard 'Figure 1-a' form. The Figure 2 note's significance legend does not specify that the stars attach to the fitted slope rather than to the plotted coefficients. None of these is serious on its own; collectively they suggest a light copyedit.

NAVIGABILITY VERDICT. The load-bearing material is roughly 700 words — the two Results subsections — plus Figure 2. The Introduction is standard framing and can be skipped except for the Chapter 74 definition. The Data section is skimmable except for the concentrator definition, which is needed to interpret every exhibit. The Discussion's first paragraph (female) adds little beyond Results; its second and third (Hispanic, ELL) carry the interpretive claims and should be read, with the caveat that both lean on unseen appendix figures. The paper is a good, fast read that is easy to over-quote; the specific places to slow down are the abstract's ELL sentence, the 'converged toward zero' sentence, the Hispanic representation sentence next to Figure 1(e), and the two figure notes' disagreeing cohort ranges.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

A compact, well-executed descriptive brief that establishes a genuinely new empirical fact base: a 15-cohort (2010–2024), full-census series of Massachusetts Chapter 74 participation and concentration disaggregated by demographic group, showing that high-quality CTE grew from ~15% to ~20% while any-CTE stayed flat, and that this growth was distributionally uneven — improving for female and Black students, stagnant for Hispanic/Latino students and ELLs despite those groups' rapid population growth. Its most distinctive finding, that within-school/town adjusted disparities converged toward zero for female and Hispanic students but widened for ELLs, is new and provocative. Its most quotable claim — that Hispanic underrepresentation is an access problem while ELL underrepresentation is a within-school problem — is an interpretation of the contrast between two figures rather than a tested decomposition, and outruns what the paper demonstrates.

**Strengths:**

- The 15-cohort census series is the paper's real asset. No prior source — the authors' own Massachusetts work (Dougherty & Macdonald 2019/2020; Dougherty 2025), the multi-state Goldring et al. (2021) trend report, or DESE's own reporting — provides a window this long, on the full state population (1.1M students, 377 comprehensive + 36 wall-to-wall schools), disaggregated simultaneously by demographic group AND by the participation/concentration distinction AND by the Chapter 74 vs. Perkins-only quality tier. That four-way cut over 15 cohorts is the contribution readers should value most.
- The framing of high-quality CTE growth as a distributional question rather than an aggregate one is the right question at the right time. The finding that any-CTE participation was flat while Chapter 74 rose implies conversion of existing offerings rather than net expansion — a zero-sum reallocation under fixed capacity. That reframing, combined with rising Grade 8 baseline achievement among entrants (Figure A2), gives readers a coherent and policy-relevant account of what 'quality upgrading under excess demand' actually does to a system.
- The ELL divergence is the paper's genuinely novel empirical result. Prior Massachusetts CTE work in this literature has centered race/ethnicity, gender, SWD status, and program availability; ELL status as a distinct and worsening axis is not established elsewhere, and the Figure A7 check within the Hispanic population (separating linguistic access from ethnicity) is exactly the right test to make it credible rather than a proxy for the Hispanic finding.
- The Perkins-only contrast (Figure A9) — muted demographic associations, no cohort trend — is the most conceptually generative thing in the brief. It converts a single-state descriptive finding into a testable general hypothesis: that inequity is a feature of the selective tier specifically, not of CTE generally. That is the kind of claim that sets up follow-on work in other states, and it is what makes this brief worth more than a state fact sheet.
- The paper is honest about being descriptive. It uses 'association,' 'suggests,' 'may,' and 'points to' consistently, and never claims causal identification. The overreach risk here is in how the paper will be read and cited, not in what it asserts.

**Weaknesses:**

- The central interpretive move — 'Hispanic underrepresentation is about access, ELL underrepresentation is about within-school barriers' — rests on an informal eyeball comparison of Figure 1 (raw trends) against Figure 2 (FE-adjusted trends). The paper calls it a 'decomposition approach,' but no decomposition is performed: there is no partition of variance into between- versus within-school components, no formal test of whether the ELL slope differs from the others, and no direct measurement of either proposed mechanism (no program-supply-per-town measures, no language-support or program-offering-mix data, no application, waitlist, or admissions records). The mechanism story is a plausible reading of a residual, not a result.
- The magnitudes cut against the framing. In Figure 2 the ELL adjusted coefficient moves from roughly zero in 2010 to about -0.018 by 2023, against a raw ELL participation gap on the order of 10 percentage points in Figure 1(h). So the school and town fixed effects plus observables absorb the large majority of ELL underrepresentation, and the within-school residual — the thing the paper's headline emphasizes — is the small remainder. 'Widening' is defensible; 'ELLs face persistent within-school barriers' as a primary characterization gives a 1–2pp residual more weight than its size supports.
- The adjusted models condition on Grade 8 math achievement and attendance. Because Chapter 74 programs, particularly at oversubscribed wall-to-wall schools, may screen applicants on precisely these measures, the FE estimates are gaps net of the main selection channel. The regression therefore cannot speak to the selectivity mechanism the Discussion invokes; it estimates what remains after that mechanism has operated. This makes the within-school estimates conservative for policy purposes but also means they do not measure what a reader might assume they measure.
- It is unclear whether the 36 wall-to-wall CTE schools enter the fixed-effects models, and this matters a great deal. At a wall-to-wall school, essentially every student is a Chapter 74 participant, so Grade 9 school fixed effects come close to absorbing the outcome. If those schools are included, the FE coefficients are identified largely off within-wall-to-wall variation in concentrating versus merely participating; if excluded, the 'within-school' story is a story about comprehensive high schools only. Either way, the within-school analysis is not analyzing the setting where the oversubscription and selective-admissions pressure the introduction foregrounds.
- Substantial repackaging of the authors' own prior Massachusetts work. That only one-fifth of comprehensive high schools offer any Chapter 74 program, that wall-to-wall schools are heavily oversubscribed, and that expanding technical education availability affects participation equality are established in Dougherty & Macdonald (2019, 2020), Dougherty (2025), and the companion Yoon & Dougherty (2026) SSRN paper. The brief cites these appropriately, but a reader should recognize that the access-constraint premise is inherited, not demonstrated here — what is new is the long disaggregated trend series and the ELL result.
- The Brief format is doing real damage to citability. There are no tables, no reported sample sizes by group or cohort, no coefficient values in the text, and nine of the eleven exhibits — including the Perkins-only contrast that anchors the concluding argument, the Grade 8 school FE robustness check, the program-mix evidence for the ELL language-demand mechanism, and the participation-outcome robustness check — live in an online appendix. Readers cannot evaluate several load-bearing claims from the published article itself.
- The 2010–2024 window spans a period of active change in Massachusetts vocational school admissions policy, including state-level revisions constraining selective admissions criteria and an ongoing debate over lottery admissions for oversubscribed programs. The brief never mentions this. Readers should not treat the cohort series as tracking behavior under a fixed policy regime, and any inflection in the later cohorts is difficult to interpret without that context.
- 'High-quality' is an administrative label throughout — Chapter 74 state approval, 900+ hours, employer partnership, credential opportunity. The paper asserts a 'quality premium' by citation rather than establishing it, and studies participation only, never outcomes. The title and framing invite readers to treat this as evidence about high-quality CTE in an outcome sense, which it is not.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR the descriptive trend facts, which are its best-supported and most durable contribution: that Massachusetts Chapter 74 participation rose from roughly 15% to 20% across the 2010–2024 on-time graduation cohorts while any-CTE participation stayed flat and Perkins-only participation and offerings declined; and that baseline Grade 8 achievement among entrants rose over the same period. This is a full-census series and is currently the best available long-run evidence of its kind.
- CITE IT FOR the disaggregated composition finding: female and Black/African American students' Chapter 74 participation and concentration grew faster than the statewide rate, while Hispanic/Latino and ELL participation was flat and therefore did not scale with those groups' substantial population growth. This is a clean, well-measured fact about a full population.
- CITE IT FOR the ELL divergence as a documented anomaly worth investigating — the within-school/town adjusted gap for ELLs widened across cohorts while every other group's stayed flat or converged toward zero, and this holds within the Hispanic population. This is the paper's most original empirical result and the best reason to read it.
- CITE IT CAUTIOUSLY, as a hypothesis rather than a finding, for the claim that inequities are a distinctive feature of selective high-quality pathways relative to Perkins-only programs. The supporting evidence is a single appendix figure (A9) from one state, with no formal comparison test.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT for the claim that Hispanic/Latino underrepresentation is driven by access while ELL underrepresentation is driven by within-school barriers. Reason: the attribution is inferred from the visual contrast between raw and fixed-effects-adjusted trends, with no formal decomposition and no measurement of either proposed mechanism.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT for a claim that ELLs face large within-school barriers to high-quality CTE. Reason: the adjusted within-school gap reaches only about 1.5–2 percentage points at its widest, against a raw gap several times that size — most ELL underrepresentation is between schools and towns, not within them.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT for anything about the effects, returns, or outcomes of high-quality CTE. Reason: the paper measures participation and concentration only; 'high-quality' here is the Chapter 74 regulatory designation, and the quality premium is asserted by citation, not tested. For causal questions about access expansion, cite the companion Yoon & Dougherty (2026) SSRN paper instead.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT for national or cross-state generalization. Reason: Massachusetts' combination of a state-approved quality tier plus 36 selective wall-to-wall regional vocational technical schools is close to unique in the US, and the specific access-constraint dynamic driving these results is a product of that architecture.
- OPEN QUESTIONS a reader should know remain unresolved: whether the wall-to-wall schools are included in the fixed-effects models, and therefore what 'within-school' actually refers to; whether the widening ELL gap reflects language-responsive support deficits, program-mix shifts toward English-intensive sectors, admissions screening, or student and family preferences, none of which is measured; how much of the pattern is an artifact of Massachusetts' evolving vocational admissions regulations over the study window; whether the Perkins-only contrast replicates in states with different quality-tier structures; and whether the participation disparities documented here translate into disparities in outcomes.
- READERS SHOULD RETRIEVE THE ONLINE APPENDIX before citing anything beyond Figures 1 and 2. Figures A1–A9 carry the Perkins-only contrast, the Grade 8 school FE robustness check, the program-mix evidence, and the participation-outcome check — several of the Discussion's central claims are not verifiable from the six published pages.

**Detailed Commentary:**

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW

Three things, in descending order of solidity.

First, and most valuable, the fact base. Fifteen on-time graduation cohorts covering 1.1 million students — the full Massachusetts public high school population — with Chapter 74 participation and concentration separated, Perkins-only separated, and everything cut by gender, race/ethnicity, disability status, and ELL status. Prior Massachusetts work from this team covered shorter windows and narrower questions (Dougherty & Macdonald 2020 on STEM program availability; Dougherty & Macdonald 2019 and Dougherty 2025 on excess demand), and Goldring et al. (2021) is multi-state but does not resolve a state's internal quality tier this way. The 15-cohort disaggregated series is a public good, and it is the thing the paper should become the reference for.

Second, the ELL finding. Every other group in Figure 2 is flat or converging toward zero; ELLs alone diverge, with a statistically significant negative slope (-0.0010*). The Figure A7 check within the Hispanic population is the right move and makes this substantially more credible than a bare interaction. I am not aware of prior work establishing this, and it is the most quotable genuinely-new result in the paper.

Third, and weakest, the analytic framing: plotting cohort-by-cohort fixed-effects coefficients as a time series and reading the raw-versus-adjusted contrast as an access-versus-sorting diagnostic. This is a sensible descriptive device, but it is a framing rather than a method, and the paper's use of the word 'decomposition' oversells it.

WHAT REPACKAGES PRIOR WORK

The entire premise — that Chapter 74 is oversubscribed, that only about one-fifth of comprehensive high schools offer it, that access is the binding constraint — is inherited from the authors' own prior Massachusetts output and asserted by citation in the first two paragraphs. The aggregate Chapter 74 growth trend is likely already visible in DESE reporting. The gender-representation improvement echoes the 2020 JVET paper's question directly. None of this is improper; the citations are there. But a reader deciding what is new should locate the novelty in the length and granularity of the series and in the ELL result, not in the framing.

THE QUOTABLE-VERSUS-SUPPORTED GAP

This is the most important thing for a reader to internalize about this paper.

The claim this paper will be cited for is the abstract's closing sentence: Hispanic underrepresentation is tied to school access and choice, whereas ELLs face persistent within-school barriers. It is clean, it is mechanistic, it maps onto two different policy levers, and it is exactly the kind of sentence that gets pulled into literature reviews and policy briefs.

The claim this paper actually supports is: over 15 cohorts, Chapter 74 participation grew, that growth was demographically uneven, and the pattern of within-school residual gaps differs across groups in a way that is suggestive of different mechanisms.

The distance between those two is the informal comparison of Figure 1 against Figure 2. There is no variance decomposition, no test of slope differences across groups, no measure of program supply by town, no measure of language-responsive supports, no admissions or waitlist data. The Figure A6 robustness check (Grade 8 school FE substituted for high school FE) is a genuine and useful strengthening of the Hispanic access story, and I credit it. But 'the residual shrinks, therefore the action is in access' is an inference from what a regression fails to explain, and residuals are agnostic about their sources.

The magnitude problem compounds this. Reading Figure 2 panel (f), the ELL coefficient goes from roughly zero in 2010 to about -0.018 by 2023. Figure 1 panel (h) shows ELL Chapter 74 participation running well below the statewide ~20%. So the school and town fixed effects plus the observable controls absorb the large majority of the raw ELL gap, and the paper's headline within-school story concerns the small remaining piece. The trend in that piece is real and worth reporting. But a reader who cites this for 'ELLs face substantial within-school barriers to high-quality CTE' has inverted the paper's own evidence about where the bulk of ELL underrepresentation sits.

A related interpretive trap: because the models condition on Grade 8 math achievement, the estimated gaps are net of the achievement-based screening that selective Chapter 74 admissions plausibly use. The within-school ELL gap is therefore a residual on top of the selection channel, not a measure of it — which makes it conservative, but also means it is not the quantity a policy reader is likely to think they are reading.

THE WALL-TO-WALL AMBIGUITY

The brief never states whether the 36 wall-to-wall CTE schools are in the fixed-effects models. This is consequential. At a wall-to-wall school, Chapter 74 participation is close to universal, so a Grade 9 school fixed effect nearly absorbs the outcome; the identifying variation would be concentrating versus merely participating. If they are excluded, then the 'within-school' analysis describes sorting inside comprehensive high schools — while the oversubscription and selective-admissions pressure that motivates the entire paper lives at the wall-to-wall schools. Either reading leaves a gap between the mechanism the introduction describes and the setting the regressions analyze. A reader should not assume the within-school estimates speak to admissions selectivity at the selective schools.

FORMAT CONSTRAINTS ON CITABILITY

Six pages, two figures, no tables, no reported coefficient values in text, no by-group sample sizes. Nine appendix exhibits carry claims that appear in the Discussion as conclusions: the Perkins-only contrast (A9) that anchors the final paragraph, the Grade 8 school FE check (A6) that anchors the Hispanic access story, the program-mix evidence (A8) that anchors the ELL language-demand mechanism, and the participation robustness check (A5). Anyone citing the Discussion's arguments is citing the appendix, and should read it. This is a constraint of the venue and format rather than a flaw in the work, but it should govern how confidently the paper is invoked.

GENERALIZABILITY

The paper is reasonably careful in the body — it repeatedly says 'in Massachusetts' and explains why Massachusetts is distinctive. But the introduction's closing promise of 'direct implications for the growing number of states pursuing their own program investments' and the Discussion's 'broader challenge facing high-quality CTE systems' both invite extension that the design cannot support. Massachusetts' architecture — a formal state quality designation plus a network of selective regional vocational technical schools with independent admissions — is close to unique. The transportable claim is conditional and hypothesis-shaped: where a state creates a selective quality tier under binding capacity constraints, expect the composition of that tier to diverge from the population, and expect access rather than in-school sorting to be the dominant margin. That is a genuinely useful proposition for other states to test. It is not a finding about them.

A further caution: the 2010–2024 window overlaps a period of active state-level change in Massachusetts vocational admissions policy, including regulatory constraints on selective admissions criteria and a public debate over lottery-based admissions for oversubscribed programs. The brief does not mention this. Readers should treat the later cohorts as observed under a shifting regime rather than a stable one, which matters especially for the endpoint values that will get quoted.

STANDING AND FOLLOW-ON WORK

Within its niche this is now the best available longitudinal descriptive evidence on the demographic composition of a state's selective high-quality CTE tier, and it should displace shorter-window state trend reports for that purpose. It sits alongside rather than above Jacob & Ricks (2023), which addresses the preferences-versus-availability question with an identification strategy this paper lacks; readers wanting that question answered rather than posed should go there. For causal questions about what expanding Chapter 74 access does, the companion SSRN paper is the right citation, and this brief is best understood as its descriptive front-end.

The follow-on agenda it sets up is clear and worth stating, because it is part of the contribution: (1) the ELL mechanism, which requires program-level offering data, language-support measures, and ideally application records — the paper's own Figure A8 conjecture about growth in English-intensive sectors like education and health services is directly testable; (2) whether the selective-tier-versus-Perkins-only contrast replicates in other states, which would convert a state observation into a design principle; (3) whether Massachusetts' admissions-policy changes moved these gaps, which the 15-cohort series is well-positioned to support as a quasi-experimental design; and (4) whether these participation gaps translate into outcome gaps.

BOTTOM LINE FOR READERS

A useful, honest, well-measured brief whose descriptive contribution is solid and worth citing, and whose mechanistic contribution is a hypothesis dressed in the grammar of a finding. Cite the trends with confidence, cite the ELL divergence as an important open puzzle, and do not let the abstract's tidy access-versus-within-school dichotomy travel further than the two figures behind it can carry it.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The Brief names its data source with unusual precision (Massachusetts DESE student-level records, 1,112,121 students across 15 on-time graduation cohorts, 377 comprehensive and 36 wall-to-wall schools) and anchors its key exposure variable to a citable external standard, but it contains no data availability statement, no described access pathway, no replication code or software, and no Methods section or estimating equation. Every quantitative claim in the paper must be read off two figures: there is not a single table, coefficient, standard error, or per-cohort N in the main text, and the sample definition, demographic measurement timing, and 15-year harmonization of test scores and lunch eligibility are all undocumented. A reader cannot check the numbers, and a replicator holding the same DESE file would have to guess at a half-dozen construction choices that plausibly move the headline ELL result.

**Strengths:**

- The data source is named exactly and dimensioned: agency (Massachusetts DESE), unit (student-level), span (on-time graduation cohorts 2010-2024), universe (1,112,121 students; 377 comprehensive + 36 wall-to-wall CTE schools), and content (demographics, school ID, town of residence, Grade 8 standardized test scores, Grades 9-12 CTE participation records separately flagged Perkins-only vs. Chapter 74). A replicator knows precisely which agency and which universe to request, which is more than many administrative-data briefs provide.
- The central exposure variable rests on public, external definitions rather than author judgment. 'High-quality' is the state's own Chapter 74 program approval (with its 900-hour, employer-partnership, and credential criteria stated in the text), and 'concentrator' is tied to the federal Perkins V framework operationalized as two or more academic years in a Chapter 74 program following Goldring et al. (2021) — a cited, retrievable source a replicator can consult for the coding rule.
- The Figure 2 note carries more specification content than the body text and is doing real work: it names the model class (linear probability models), both fixed-effect dimensions, the named controls (baseline Grade 8 math achievement, Grade 8 attendance rate, FRPL eligibility, all major demographics), the per-cohort estimation structure, and 95% confidence intervals with significance thresholds. For a six-page Brief with no Methods section, this is the difference between partially and wholly opaque.
- Robustness and mechanism checks are enumerated specifically rather than gestured at, and each is mapped to a numbered supplemental figure: A5 (participation as the alternative outcome), A6 (Grade 8 school fixed effects replacing high school), A7 (widening ELL gap within the Hispanic population), A8 (program-area composition of the Chapter 74 expansion), A9 (Perkins-only contrast). A reader knows what was run and where to look.
- Supplemental material is deposited online with the article rather than promised on request, and a companion working paper on the same data (Yoon & Dougherty, 2026; SSRN 6366869, DOI given) is publicly posted and cited — giving readers two concrete places to pursue the documentation the Brief omits.

**Weaknesses:**

- There is no data availability statement anywhere in the article. I searched the full text: the front matter, the Data section, and the back matter (Acknowledgments, ORCID, Funding, Declaration of Conflicting Interests, Supplemental Material) contain no statement about data access, no mention of a DESE data-use agreement or research partnership agreement, no IRB or human-subjects statement, and no guidance on whether an unaffiliated researcher could obtain the same file. The only trace of the access pathway is an acknowledgment of DESE's 'generous support and partnership' — which tells a reader that access ran through a relationship, not through a documented, followable procedure. Restricted administrative data legitimately cannot be posted; that is not the failing. The failing is that the article does not say the data are restricted, does not say under what instrument they were obtained, and does not say what a replicator would have to do.
- There is no replication code, no repository or deposit, no named statistical software or version, and no statement explaining the absence. Nothing here is computationally exotic — these are linear probability models with two fixed-effect dimensions, so no priors, samplers, or seeds are at issue — but that also means there is no technical obstacle to depositing the do-files or scripts that construct the sample and produce the two figures. Code can be posted even when data cannot, and a construction script would resolve most of the ambiguities listed below at zero disclosure cost.
- The article has no Methods section and no estimating equation. The specification exists only as a sentence of body prose and a figure note, and the two do not fully agree: the text says 'high school and town-of-residence fixed effects,' the Figure 2 note says 'Grade 9 school fixed effect and town fixed effect,' and the Discussion describes A6 as 'replacing high school with Grade 8 school fixed effects.' Whether 'high school' means the Grade 9 school of record, the Grade 12 school, or a modal school is never stated, and it matters directly for movers and for students who enter a wall-to-wall school at Grade 9. Also unstated: whether one LPM is fit per cohort or a pooled model with cohort interactions is used (the phrasing 'for each on-time graduation cohort' implies the former, but it is inference); how standard errors are computed and at what level they are clustered; whether observations are weighted; whether all demographics are entered jointly and which is the omitted race category; and how missing Grade 8 scores or attendance are handled (dropped, imputed, or flagged).
- The analytic sample is undefined. 'On-time graduation cohort' is used throughout and never operationalized, and the two natural readings differ materially. If it means students who actually graduated on time, the sample conditions on an outcome that CTE participation may itself affect and that is differentially attained by ELL, Hispanic/Latino, and SWD students — so the headline trend in ELL concentration would be partly confounded by changes over 15 cohorts in who survives to on-time graduation. If it means expected graduation year (Grade 9 entry plus four), the sample is a full entry cohort and that concern largely evaporates. The reported 1,112,121 over 15 cohorts (~74,100 per cohort) is consistent with either reading given Massachusetts enrollment, so the count does not disambiguate it. Nothing in the text tells a replicator which students are dropped, how transfers in and out of state are handled, whether the 377 + 36 school set is fixed across all 15 cohorts or is the union of schools ever observed (schools opened and closed over this window), or how students in non-comprehensive, non-wall-to-wall settings (charters, vocational-adjacent, alternative programs) are treated.
- Measurement timing for the paper's central variables is never stated. ELL, SWD, and FRPL status are point-in-time designations in DESE records, and the paper does not say whether they are measured in Grade 8, at Grade 9 entry, at any point in high school, or 'ever.' This is not a technicality for this particular paper: Massachusetts reclassifies students out of ELL status as they attain proficiency, so an ever-ELL definition and a Grade 8 point-in-time definition produce populations that differ in size and in composition, and can trend in different directions across cohorts. The headline finding is a widening ELL concentration gap across cohorts; that finding's sign and slope are sensitive to a definitional choice the article does not disclose. 'Town of residence' — the fixed effect carrying the entire Hispanic/Latino access interpretation — is likewise undefined for movers.
- No harmonization is documented across a 15-year window containing at least three known measurement breaks in the variables the models control for. (a) Grade 8 math: legacy MCAS gave way to Next-Generation MCAS in grades 3-8 in spring 2017, which corresponds to roughly the 2021 graduation cohort, so cohorts 2010-2020 and 2021-2023 sit on different tests. The article says only 'standardized state test scores in Grade 8' — no standardization metric (within cohort? within cohort-grade? statewide pooled?), no mention of the transition. (b) Spring 2020 MCAS was cancelled outright and Grade 8 attendance for 2019-20 was disrupted by school closures, which affects exactly the 2024 graduation cohort. (c) FRPL: DESE replaced free/reduced-price lunch with an 'economically disadvantaged' measure after 2014-15 as Community Eligibility Provision adoption spread, so the stated FRPL control changes meaning partway through the panel. All three breaks fall inside the estimation window and touch controls that carry the adjusted-coefficient trends, and none is acknowledged.
- There are no numeric results reported anywhere in the main text — no table, no coefficient magnitude, no standard error, no per-cohort sample size, no model fit statistic. The only two numbers in the results narrative are 'roughly 15 to 20 percent' Chapter 74 participation and 'about two-thirds of all ELLs' being Hispanic. Everything else must be recovered by eye from Figure 1 and Figure 2. The paper's headline claims are trend claims — the female and Hispanic/Latino coefficients 'steadily converged toward zero,' the ELL disparity 'has widened' — but the fitted lines in Figure 2 are described only as summarizing 'the cohort trend,' with no estimation method, no slope, no standard error, and no test. The asterisks in the note attach to individual per-cohort coefficients, not to the trends the article actually argues for. As reported, the central claims are visual.
- Figure 1 runs through the 2024 cohort but Figure 2 stops at 2023, and the article never says why. The most likely explanation is that the Grade 8 controls do not exist for the 2024 graduation cohort (Grade 8 in 2019-20, when MCAS was cancelled and attendance collapsed), but a reader has to reconstruct that; an unexplained one-cohort truncation in the regression figure, in a paper whose claim is about the cohort trend, should not be left to inference.
- The claim structure is heavily appendix-loaded relative to what the main text supports. Nine online-only figures carry the statewide any-CTE baseline (A1), the rising-achievement premise (A2), the demographic growth premise (A3-A4), every robustness check (A5, A6), and both mechanism arguments — that the ELL barrier is linguistic rather than ethnic (A7), that the expansion concentrated in language-demanding program areas (A8), and that inequities are distinctive to high-quality rather than Perkins-only pathways (A9). The main text is not self-verifying on any of these. Moreover, if the supplement follows the main text's own convention (figures with notes, no tables), then the appendix will not supply the Ns, standard errors, or specification detail needed to check them either — the robustness claims would then be uncheckable at any level of effort short of contacting the authors.
- The 36 wall-to-wall CTE schools, where Chapter 74 enrollment is near-universal by construction, are pooled with 377 comprehensive high schools under school fixed effects. The 'within-school' association is therefore a weighted blend of within-comprehensive variation (where concentrating is a real choice among offered programs) and within-wall-to-wall variation (where nearly everyone concentrates and the residual variation is of a different kind). Neither the weights nor the split of identifying variation is reported, and the paper's interpretive language — 'less likely to concentrate than their within-school peers' — means quite different things in the two settings.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat Figure 2 as directional evidence only. No point estimate, standard error, or per-cohort N is recoverable from what is published, so do not cite magnitudes from this paper, do not benchmark other estimates against it, and do not enter it into a meta-analysis or evidence synthesis. What is citable is the sign and the qualitative shape of the trends, conditional on the specification questions below.
- Before relying on the headline claim that ELL disparities widened, request three things from the authors: (1) when ELL status is measured (Grade 8, Grade 9 entry, or ever-ELL), (2) the per-cohort count of ELL students and ELL concentrators, and (3) the ELL trend re-estimated under the alternative ELL definition. Massachusetts reclassifies students out of ELL status, so a point-in-time and an ever-ELL definition can trend in opposite directions across 15 cohorts. This is the single most consequential undocumented choice in the paper.
- Ask how Grade 8 math achievement was standardized and whether the legacy-to-Next-Generation MCAS transition was handled explicitly. The first Next-Gen Grade 8 administration (spring 2017) corresponds to roughly the 2021 graduation cohort — that is, to the last three points of Figure 2, which are precisely the points driving the claimed ELL divergence. Ask specifically for the ELL trend re-estimated (a) dropping the achievement control entirely and (b) with within-cohort standardization, and treat the ELL result as provisional until you see that the divergence survives. The same caution applies to Figure A2's claim that baseline achievement 'has risen,' which is only interpretable once you know whether scores are standardized within cohort (in which case the claim is relative, not absolute) or on a pooled metric spanning two different tests.
- Ask why Figure 2 ends at the 2023 cohort while Figure 1 ends at 2024. The plausible reason is that the Grade 8 controls are unavailable for the 2024 cohort (Grade 8 in 2019-20, when MCAS was cancelled and attendance was disrupted), but confirm rather than assume — if the truncation instead reflects incomplete Grade 12 CTE records or a data-cut boundary, the completeness of the 2024 point in Figure 1 becomes questionable too. Either way, note that the regression trend claims rest on 14 cohort points, not 15.
- Ask what 'on-time graduation cohort' means operationally, and specifically whether the sample conditions on actually graduating on time. If it does, the analysis conditions on a post-treatment outcome that differs sharply by ELL, Hispanic/Latino, and SWD status, and the widening ELL coefficient could partly reflect a changing composition of who reaches on-time graduation rather than a changing barrier to concentrating. Ask for the analysis rerun on a Grade 9 entry cohort before treating the ELL trend as a statement about access.
- Ask how standard errors are computed and at what level they are clustered. With roughly 74,000 students per cohort and both school and town fixed effects, student-level or unclustered errors would make the 95% intervals in Figure 2 substantially too narrow, and the per-cohort significance stars in the note would be correspondingly overstated. Also ask for the estimation method and standard error of the fitted trend lines, since 'steadily converged' and 'have widened' are the paper's actual claims and no test of either is reported.
- Read the supplement before citing any robustness or mechanism claim. A5 (participation outcome), A6 (Grade 8 school fixed effects), A7 (widening gap within the Hispanic population), and A9 (Perkins-only contrast) each carry a distinct argument the main text asserts but does not support. If the supplemental figures follow the main text's convention and report no Ns, coefficients, or standard errors, then those claims are also uncheckable as published — in which case the A9-based conclusion that inequity is 'a more distinctive feature of high-quality pathways' should be reported as the authors' assertion, not as a verified contrast.
- Consult the companion working paper (Yoon & Dougherty, 2026, SSRN 6366869) before relying on this Brief alone. It uses the same DESE data and, as a full-length paper, likely contains the sample construction, estimating equation, variable definitions, and tables this Brief omits. Verify that its definitions match the Brief's before importing them — and if they differ, treat the Brief's undocumented choices as unresolved rather than assuming the companion's apply.
- A partial independent check is possible without restricted access, and it is worth doing. DESE publicly posts school-level Chapter 74 program approvals and district- and school-level enrollment and vocational participation data. From these you can approximately verify the descriptive supply-side claims — that roughly one-fifth of comprehensive high schools offer any Chapter 74 program, that the number of schools offering Perkins-only programs declined, and the rough shape of the statewide 15-to-20-percent Chapter 74 participation increase. What you cannot check without the restricted student-level file is Figure 2, the within-school and within-town adjusted associations, which is the paper's actual analytic contribution. Distinguish the two layers when citing: the descriptive layer is externally corroborable, the adjusted layer is entirely on trust.
- Note that the free-or-reduced-price-lunch control changes definition mid-panel — Massachusetts moved to an 'economically disadvantaged' measure after 2014-15 as Community Eligibility Provision adoption spread, which mechanically altered who is flagged low-income. Ask how this was harmonized across the 2010-2024 span. A control whose meaning shifts around 2015 sits inside every adjusted cohort coefficient, and an unaddressed break there could itself generate an apparent trend in the demographic coefficients.

**Detailed Commentary:**

I read the complete published article text and independently re-extracted the PDF to confirm absences rather than infer them from a possibly lossy extraction. Searching the full document for 'availab', 'replicat', 'repositor', 'deposit', 'Stata', 'R version', 'Python', 'IRB', 'restricted', 'agreement', 'open science', 'OSF', 'GitHub', 'Dataverse', 'upon request', 'seed', and 'code' returns only four hits, none of them a transparency statement: 'programs are available at a given time' (body prose), 'Supplemental material for this article is available online,' and two occurrences inside reference titles. The article's structure is Introduction, Data, Results, Discussion — there is no Methods section — and the back matter runs Acknowledgments, ORCID iDs, Funding, Declaration of Conflicting Interests, Supplemental Material, References, Author Biographies. So the negative findings here are confirmed, not assumed.

On calibration. The instruction to credit restricted-access data is the right frame, and I have applied it: I am not penalizing these authors for failing to post a Massachusetts student-level census. The problem is a different one. Restricted data constrain sharing; they do not constrain describing. Nothing about a DESE data agreement prevents the article from saying which instrument governed access and whether another researcher could seek the same, from stating the estimating equation, from reporting per-cohort Ns and standard errors in a supplemental table, from saying whether ELL is measured in Grade 8 or ever, or from noting that Grade 8 math crosses the Next-Gen MCAS transition mid-panel. Each of those is a sentence or a small table, and the article contains none of them. Brief format is a real constraint on the body text, but it is not a constraint on the supplement, which already holds nine figures and could equally have held a construction appendix, nor on the back matter, where a data availability statement costs three lines. Educational Researcher is a journal-era publication with an accepted date of June 2026; a data availability statement and either a deposited replication package or a stated reason for its absence are reasonable expectations that go unmet here.

On why this lands at 'weak' rather than 'adequate.' Consider what a replicator with a signed DESE agreement and the identical raw files would face. To rebuild the analytic sample they would need to decide: what defines an on-time graduation cohort and which students are dropped; whether the 377 + 36 school frame is fixed or the union across years; how transfers, movers, and mid-year enrollees are assigned to a Grade 9 school and a town; whether ELL, SWD, and FRPL are point-in-time or ever measures and at which grade; how 'participated in a Chapter 74 program for two or more academic years' handles program switching, partial-year enrollment, and wall-to-wall students for whom Chapter 74 enrollment is structural rather than elective; which DESE field distinguishes Chapter 74 from Perkins-only enrollment at the student level; how Grade 8 math is standardized and how the legacy-to-Next-Gen break and the 2020 cancellation are handled; how FRPL is defined after the 2015 shift to 'economically disadvantaged'; and, on the estimation side, whether models are per-cohort or pooled with interactions, what the omitted race category is, how missing controls are handled, whether observations are weighted, and at what level errors are clustered. That is well over a dozen consequential choices, several of which — the sample definition and the ELL measurement timing in particular — could plausibly reverse or flatten the paper's headline result. A replication under those conditions would not be a replication; it would be a new study that happens to share a data source.

On why it is not 'insufficient.' The floor here is genuinely higher than nothing. The data source is named with agency, unit, span, and exact counts, so there is no ambiguity about what universe to request. The key exposure variable is a state administrative designation rather than an author-constructed index, and the concentrator rule is delegated to a published, citable source (Goldring et al., 2021), so the single most important coding decision in the paper is externally documented even though its implementation is not. The Figure 2 note names the model class, both fixed-effect dimensions, and the full control list. Robustness checks are individually named and mapped to figures rather than waved at. And a publicly posted companion paper on the same data exists and is cited, giving a diligent reader somewhere concrete to go. That combination distinguishes this from a paper whose central results cannot even be located, which is what 'insufficient' should mean.

One structural observation worth flagging to readers separately from the specification issues. The verifiable core of this Brief is thin relative to its claim structure. Of the article's substantive assertions, the ones a reader can check against public DESE data are the supply-side descriptives — Chapter 74 program availability by school, the decline in Perkins-only offerings, the approximate statewide participation trend. Everything the paper is actually contributing — the demographic-specific cohort trends in Figure 1, and above all the adjusted within-school, within-town associations in Figure 2 — rests on a restricted file with no published numbers attached, and its robustness rests further on nine figures the article does not reproduce. The two mechanism claims that give the paper its policy punch, that Hispanic/Latino underrepresentation is an access-and-sorting phenomenon while the ELL gap is a within-school phenomenon, follow from contrasting Figure 1 against Figure 2 and are reinforced only by supplemental figures A6 and A7. A reader who wants to lean on that contrast is leaning on two graphs and an appendix, with no reported estimate, interval, or sample size behind any of it. The findings may well be right — the design is sensible and the authors have a track record on these data — but 'may well be right' is the correct epistemic posture here, and readers should adopt it explicitly rather than treating the ELL result as an established fact about Massachusetts CTE.
